solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ideas you don't want advanced; this is probably the 13th

indicators.note: what you don't want is left out, so a letter is struck from the word Ideas

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for advanced, as in A level

explanation.surface: A warning against pushing ideas forward, with a hint about a date.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Roman calendar the Ides fell on the 13th of most months, the 15th only in March, May, July and October, hence 'probably'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman calendar's mid-month day, which in eight of the twelve months fell on the thirteenth.

clue.text: Recognising inflexion of verb too is a noun

indicators.note: an inflexion bends or alters a word's form, so the letters of verb too is a are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
N is the grammarian's abbreviation for noun

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson: the way a verb changes shows it is really a noun.
explanation.walkthrough: The grammar vocabulary (inflexion, verb, noun) makes the clue read like a linguistics note; 'inflexion of' is an unusual anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Noticing or perceiving something is the act of watching it closely, so recognising works as a gerund synonym.

clue.text: With day to glance round this island, pass slowly

indicators.note: the word for glance goes round the island's letters

parts.note: a glance can be a ray, as a beam of light glances off a surface
GB, Great Britain, is the island the British setter and solver live on

explanation.surface: Someone glancing about Britain while the days drag on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' is just a link. The ray of light glances; it wraps round GB.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that drags by goes past tediously, the phrasal verb for slow passing of hours.

clue.text: Pot did (or not) for stewing kangaroo

indicators.note: things put in a pot for stewing get stirred and mixed, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook hesitating over whether to put a kangaroo in the pot.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is obscure; the checking letters help fix the order.
explanation.definitionFit: Diprotodont marsupials have two prominent lower front teeth, and kangaroos belong to that order, so a kangaroo is an example.

clue.text: Cover's beginning when it's gone

indicators.note: the beginning, i.e. the first letter, of the word for beginning goes, so D is dropped

parts.note: dawning means a beginning, as in the dawning of an age

explanation.surface: A cover that disappears the moment it starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning' does double duty: it is both the synonym and the letter lost from it, which the blog notes may irritate some solvers.
explanation.definitionFit: A canvas sheet stretched over a shop window or deck is a cover against sun and rain.

clue.text: Herbivore in book that's all about the home

indicators.note: all about suggests letters scattered all over, so the words the home are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A book about domestic life featuring a plant-eating animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' and 'that's' are links; the blog thought the anagram signal's placement a bit dodgy.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical beast in the Book of Job eats grass like an ox, so it is a plant-eater.

clue.text: Fussy if stalling cows

indicators.note: stalling suggests shifting or messing about, so the two letters of if swap places

parts.note: KY (or kye) is an old Scots plural of cow

explanation.surface: Fussiness over whether stalled cows will cooperate.
explanation.walkthrough: A Scots word listed in Chambers; KY, like kine, is a dialect plural for cows.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish dialect adjective for finicky or overparticular, listed in Chambers.

clue.text: The street for news of all events. Every second counts

indicators.note: every second letter of of all events is taken, the second, fourth and so on

explanation.surface: Journalism's home street reporting all events, where every second counts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every second counts' reads as a newsroom deadline cliché, but it tells you to take alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: London's former newspaper district, Fleet Street, is synonymous with the national press.

clue.text: Tops of knees indicate length tailors suggest for them

definitions.text: Tops of knees indicate length tailors suggest for them

indicators.note: the tops of words are their first letters, so the initials are read off

explanation.surface: Tailors say a Highland skirt should reach the top of the knees.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the initials spell the garment whose length is set at the knee.
explanation.definitionFit: Highland dress skirts are traditionally cut so the hem sits at the knee.

clue.text: Emirate? Name one — one suffices

parts.note: to dub is to name, as when a knight is dubbed
A means one, as in a pound
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A quiz: name one emirate, and one answer is enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' gives two different letters, A and I.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the seven states of the United Arab Emirates, and its best-known city.

clue.text: Buffoon with hook nose could be swimming up Loch Linnhe

indicators.note: swimming means moving about in water, so these letters drift into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a sea loch in western Scotland; the anagram needs its name with a single H, the second H being the setter's slip

explanation.surface: A hook-nosed clown swimming the length of a Scottish sea loch.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder as printed has one H too many; drop one H and 'could be swimming' rearranges the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The hook-nosed clown of Italian puppet theatre, ancestor of Mr Punch, is a stock buffoon.

clue.text: Here's exotic Ayesha, the Queen that's pure

parts.note: Ayesha is the exotic queen of Rider Haggard's novel She, known as She-who-must-be-obeyed
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: Introducing an exotic queen who is a model of purity.
explanation.walkthrough: Ayesha rules a lost African kingdom in Haggard's adventure novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheer means unmixed or absolute, as in sheer folly, so it means pure.

clue.text: One who decorates with gold isn't meant to be extravagant

parts.note: OR is gold in heraldry

indicators.note: extravagant means wandering beyond bounds, so the letters stray into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A decorator who gilds things without intending to overdo it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' is a link; the gold suits the surface's decorator.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who adds embellishment or ornament to objects is a decorator by trade.

clue.text: Rough men worried about doing not well where they may do better

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go about, i.e. around, the word for wrongdoing
worried means disturbed and shaken up, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
doing wrong rather than well is to sin; doing is a noun here

explanation.surface: Rough men fretting about their misdeeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doing not well' looks like ill health but means wrongdoing; the definition puns on 'do better' as getting well.
explanation.definitionFit: A residential care home where patients may recover, so get better, under nursing care.

clue.text: Really I have to be useless

parts.note: in effect means really or in practice
I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: Someone admitting they really have to be useless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Failing to produce any result means being of no use, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Criminal steals gold plate

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked, so the letters of steals are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A crook stealing a gold plate.
explanation.walkthrough: In Chambers it is both a tuft of gold threads and a plate or clasp on a vestment, hence 'gold plate'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives an ornamental plate or clasp on a church vestment, often of gold work.

clue.text: Pen store at college

parts.note: the Co-op is a British chain of cooperative stores
up means in residence at university, as in up at Oxford

explanation.surface: A store selling pens at a college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like a writing pen but is the verb to confine.
explanation.definitionFit: To shut in or confine someone in a small space, like a hen in a hutch.

clue.text: Men at work should have right to ignore soft speaker

parts.note: OR, other ranks, means men rather than officers

indicators.note: to ignore is to leave out, so the letter for soft is dropped

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work
P is piano, soft in music

explanation.surface: Workmen are told to obey their rights but ignore soft speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are joined first and only then is the P (soft) removed, which the blog called seemingly unfair but legitimate.
explanation.definitionFit: A public speaker who makes formal speeches, an eloquent declaimer.

clue.text: Streakers are unceremoniously removed for a run like this

indicators.note: the letters of are are thrown out of the pool without ceremony and the remainder is shuffled

parts.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
taken as written

explanation.surface: Streakers are hustled off the field after running in this state.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ARE out of STREAKERS, add A and R (run), then rearrange; 'like this' is how a streaker runs.
explanation.definitionFit: A streaker dashes across a pitch naked, so the colloquial word for completely nude fits.

clue.text: One who came out came without I see being excluded

parts.note: a deb, debutante, came out into society

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letters for I see are taken out

parts.note: arrived means came
I plus V, from vide, Latin for see

explanation.surface: A debutante arriving without being seen.
explanation.walkthrough: V for vide (see) is a standard reference abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Being barred or shut out from something is being kept out, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Person in irons perhaps or vice versa

definitions.text: Person in irons perhaps or vice versa

indicators.note: vice versa means the other way round, so the scrambled irons goes inside rather than outside

parts.note: PER, as in per person, stands for person

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be otherwise arranged

explanation.surface: A person in chains, or chains on a person.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads straight; then 'vice versa' turns it into instructions: irons (shuffled) in PER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone held in shackles is a captive, an example of a person in irons.

clue.text: Worthless talk from fellows cutting hair

indicators.note: cutting into means going inside, so the fellows sit within the word for hair

parts.note: pile is a soft nap or hair, as on velvet
F is fellow, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Idle chatter from men at the barber's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting hair' sounds like a barber's job.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonsense or twaddle is idle talk without value.

clue.text: Mickey's beloved mother

definitions.meaning: Mickey Mouse's sweetheart in the Disney cartoons
a Scots word for mother, listed in Chambers

explanation.surface: Mickey Mouse's sweetheart is also a dear mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Disney's cartoon girlfriend of Mickey Mouse, and a Scottish pet name for a mother.

clue.text: Discerning parental guidance about Internet surfing with adult content

indicators.note: the guidance letters go about, around, the rest

parts.note: PG is the British film rating for parental guidance

indicators.note: content means contained, so the adult letter sits inside
surfing suggests riding and tumbling, so the letters of Internet are rearranged

parts.note: A is the old certificate for adult films

explanation.surface: Parental controls on web browsing that might hit adult material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adult content' reads as web filth but means A contained in the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A penetrating mind is sharp and insightful, so discerning is a synonym.

clue.text: Chile offended Turkish ambassador

indicators.note: offended means upset, so the letters of Chile are upset into a new order

explanation.surface: A diplomatic spat in which Chile offends Turkey's envoy.
explanation.walkthrough: An obscure word from Chambers.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word, from Turkish, for an envoy or emissary, listed in Chambers.

clue.text: Hostile soldiers you once would hold up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the whole is read from bottom to top
holding means containing, so the old pronoun wraps round the soldiers

parts.note: ye is the old form of you
men means soldiers

explanation.surface: Hostile troops whom you would once have held up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold up' looks like robbery or delay but is two signals: containment and turning upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Used adjectivally, as in enemy forces, it means belonging to the opposing side.

clue.text: After golf what's next? Gleneagles?

definitions.meaning: in the NATO phonetic alphabet the word that follows golf
Gleneagles is a famous luxury golfing resort in Perthshire, Scotland

explanation.surface: A golfer wondering where to go after a round: Gleneagles?
explanation.definitionFit: Gleneagles is a grand Scottish resort establishment, and in radio spelling the code word after golf names H.

clue.text: Roll is kept by junior officer

indicators.note: kept by means held inside, so is sits within the officer's letters

parts.note: LT is lieutenant, a junior officer
taken as written

explanation.surface: A roll call held by a junior officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll' is the noun, a register of names.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll is a register or catalogue of names, such as an army roll.

clue.text: In a castle party reel can, birling with increasing speed

parts.note: C is short for castle, as on maps

indicators.note: birling is Scots for whirling, so the letters spin into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A Highland castle party with a reel danced faster and faster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link. A reel is a Scottish dance and birling is the Scots for whirling round in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical direction meaning gradually getting faster, the tempo of a quickening reel.

clue.text: Songbird — Catullus' bird — gets a thousand

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
avis is Latin for bird, the language of the poet Catullus

explanation.surface: A songbird that Catullus wrote of gains a thousand admirers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets' is a link; M goes before AVIS though the clue order suggests the reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: An old name for the song thrush, a well-known singing bird.

clue.text: Even reduction of feet in yard is fractional

indicators.note: an even reduction trims the same amount, three letters, from each end of feet in yard, leaving the middle

explanation.surface: A measuring lesson: reducing feet in a yard leaves only a fraction.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing FEE and ARD, three letters from each end, leaves the middle four.
explanation.definitionFit: Something minute or very small is a mere fraction of its whole.

clue.text: Stick had broken before

indicators.note: broken means smashed into pieces, so the letters of had are rearranged

parts.note: ere is a poetic word for before

explanation.surface: A stick that had broken earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To stick to something is to cling or cleave to it, a verb synonym.
